list.listitem: Screening colonoscopy is performed to evaluate an asymptomatic patient for cancer or polyps believed to be precursors of colorectal cancer. (CRC) There is indirect evidence from observational studies that colonoscopy reduces CRC incidence and mortality. Screening should start at the age of 45 years for any patient with no known risks. Serious harms of screening colonoscopy include perforations. (3.1/10,000 procedures) and major bleeding (14.6/10,000 procedures).

Based on the 2021 evidence report for the United States Preventive Services Task Force, the following test strategies reduce colorectal cancer (CRC)-specific mortality compared to no screening:
One-time or 2-time flexible sigmoidoscopy (incidence rate ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.68-0.80; 4 RCTs). Annual or biennial screening with guaiac-based fecal occult blood testing (relative risk [RR], 0.91; 95% CI, 0.84-0.98, at 19.5 years to RR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65-0.93, at 30 years; 5 RCTs).

This finding was confirmed and expanded in a modeling study using a population of Norwegian men and women aged 50 to 79 years with varying 15-year colorectal cancer risk. Investigators showed a reduction in CRC mortality of 6/1000 for annual fecal immunochemical testing (FIT) or single colonoscopy, 5/1000 for single sigmoidoscopy and biennial FIT and 10, 8, 4 and 1 per 1000 individuals, respectively, for colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, annual FIT, and biennial FIT among those at 3% risk of CRC.

However, in an RCT including 84,585 participants in Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and Poland who were randomized in a 1:2 ratio to receive an invitation to a single screening colonoscopy or usual care, 42% actually underwent colonoscopy and there was an absolute risk reduction in CRC incidence of -0.22% over 10 years; NNI = 455. CRC mortality, however, was not significantly lower in the screened group (0.28% vs 0.31%; RR 0.9; 0.64 -1.16) and there was no difference in all-cause mortality (11.03% vs 11.04%).

A 2024 study of more than 57,000 Spanish patients randomized them to invitation to either screening colonoscopy or fecal immunochemical testing. Uptake of both screening methods was low but better in the FIT group (20% for colonoscopy and 39% for FIT), and there was no significant difference between the incidence of colorectal cancer incidence or mortality after 10 years in the as randomized analysis.

The American College of Physicians (ACP, 2019) recommends screening for CRC using fecal occult blood testing, sigmoidoscopy, or colonoscopy in average-risk adults, beginning at the age of 50 years and continuing until the age of 75 years.A The ACP guideline also suggests presenting benefits, harms, costs, and frequencies to patients and allowing them to decide among fecal immunochemical testing (FIT) or guaiac-based fecal occult blood testing every 2 years, colonoscopy every 10 years, or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years with FIT every 2 years. Likelihood ratios for detection of colon polyps are above 10 for rigid sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, and air contrast barium enema (BE). Likelihood ratios for colon cancer in asymptomatic patients with a positive fecal occult blood are above 10 for rigid and flexible sigmoidoscopy and air contrast BE (colonoscopy was not included).

Because of a recent trend for increasing risk of colorectal cancer in birth cohorts of adults younger than 50 years, the USPSTF (2021) recommends that screening should start at age 45 years. B The American Gastroenterological Society (AGA) guidelines (2022) concur with the USPSTF to begin screening at ages 45-49 years with either colonoscopy or noninvasive approaches. No recommendations are provided on when to stop screening.
USPSTF (2021) notes that the decision to screen for CRC in adults aged 76 to 85 years should be individualized, taking into account the patient's overall health and prior screening history. C
The USPSTF (2021) continues to recommend screening colonoscopy every 10 years.

A multinational panel including patients, clinicians, content experts and methodologists developed an evidence-based guideline that found only low-level evidence of 15-year benefits, burdens and harms of CRC screening and determined that annual fecal immunochemical testing (FIT), sigmoidoscopy, or colonoscopy may reduce cancer incidence. B

Biennial FIT over 10 years was demonstrated in one study to have similar cumulative rates of detection of advanced adenomas (60 per 1000 persons) and CRC (8.5 per 1000 persons) as colonoscopy based on a screening population aged 50 to 69 years in northern Italy. The cumulative rate of positive FIT results was 25% for men and 17.6% for women.

Uptake varies across screening tests; in an RCT of 16,087 patients randomized to 1 of 4 screening approaches, the highest participation rate was for FIT testing (50%) vs. colonography (25%) or colonoscopy (12%).

One cross-sectional study found that elderly patients would like the option of continuing cancer screening beyond the age limits imposed by guidelines. In a study of Medicare beneficiaries aged 70 to 79 years, the 8-year risk for CRC was significantly reduced in the screening colonoscopy group aged 70 to 74 years over non-screened individuals (2.19% vs. 2.62%) but there was no difference in CRC in the older aged patients (2.84% vs. 2.97%, respectively).

High risk: Patients at higher risk of CRC based on their family history may benefit from earlier initiation of screening (i.e., age 40 or 45 years) although high quality evidence from clinical trials is lacking. Patients who have ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease may benefit from regular surveillance at an earlier age but studies to support this are of relatively poor quality.

The ACP recommends that screening begin at age 40 years for high-risk adults (or 10 years younger than the age at which the youngest affected relative was diagnosed with CRC). They also suggest using fecal occult blood testing or either sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy for patients at average risk, based on availability and patient risk, and colonoscopy for patients at high risk.

In patients with IBD, authors of a Cochrane review of 5 observational studies found that surveillance colonoscopy may reduce development of CRC and the rate of CRC-associated death through early detection (15/176 [8%] vs. 79/354 [22%]). Study quality, however, was poor and there were no identified RCTs.

Risk-based models including risk factors such as total calcium intake, family history, and age PLUS FIT may improve patient selection for screening colonoscopy. However, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies including 17 original risk scores among average-risk patients found relatively poor discrimination with areas under the curve of 0.61 to 0.7 in the meta-analysis.

For patients resistant to colonoscopy screening, a simple score based on age, sex and distal findings on sigmoidoscopy can be used to identify patients at low risk of having a proximal colon neoplasia (0.6%-1.0% for those found to be at low risk vs. 3.7%-4.2% for high-risk patients).

Diagnostic colonoscopy should be considered for any age patient who has unexplained symptoms such as constipation, bleeding or abdominal pain. Delay of colonoscopy after a positive FIT of more than 10 months is associated with an increased risk of CRC and advanced-stage disease. Unfortunately, in an electronic medical record study of 1267 patients with abnormal FITs, 42% failed to undergo follow-up colonoscopy within 1 year.

The 2008 European Panel on the Appropriateness of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (EPAGE) recommend diagnostic colonoscopy for the investigation of iron deficiency anemia and hematochezia in patients aged greater than or equal to 50 years, for diarrhea of greater than 4 weeks' duration, for assessing extent of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and in the face of persistent or worsening symptoms in patients with IBD. They also concluded that evidence was insufficient to support use of colonoscopy in evaluating patients with functional bowel disorders and no alarm features. Finally, they recommend colonoscopy as a first-choice procedure for surveillance after polypectomy and after curative-intent CRC resection.
In a study of referrals for colonoscopy, there was an association between high appropriateness of the indication based on EPAGE and a high diagnostic yield.

In patients with IBD, authors of a Cochrane review of 5 observational studies found that surveillance with colonoscopy may reduce development of CRC and the rate of CRC-associated death through early detection (15/176 [8%] vs. 79/354 [22%]). Study quality, however, was poor and there were no identified RCTs.

Urgent colonoscopy compared to later (after 24 hours) for patients with lower gastrointestinal bleeding does not appear to reduce mortality, rebleeding or requirement for surgery or improve identification of the bleeding source. In addition, in a retrospective review of 382 patients with hematochezia who visited a single emergency department, computed tomography evaluation was not inferior to lower endoscopy for detecting the active bleeding site.

Strategies to increase uptake of screening colonoscopy include an interactive voice response system, personalized telehealth-based risk assessment intervention, nurse-led tailored counseling, mailed outreach and provision of fecal immunochemical testing prior to colonoscopy.

In a meta-analysis of 28 studies, screening rates were higher with patient navigation for colorectal cancer overall (RR 1.64; 95% CI, 1.42-1.92; 22 trials) and specifically for colonoscopy/endoscopy (RR 2.08; 95% CI, 1.08-4.56; 6 trials). Authors noted high heterogeneity across studies.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 73 RCTs found the following risk differences (RD) for each of the screening interventions to increase the likelihood of screening uptake:
Fecal blood testing outreach, RD 22% (95% CI, 17%-27%), Patient navigation, RD 18% (95% CI, 13%-23%), Clinician reminders RD 13% (95% CI, 8%-19%), Clinician interventions of academic detailing RD 10% (95% CI, 3%-17%), Patient education RD 4% (95% CI, 1%-6%), Patient reminders RD 3% (95% CI, 0%-5%).

Offering a combination of FIT and colonoscopy as a sequential or active choice strategy increased participation in CRC screening over invitation to screening colonoscopy only in a large Polish study. Participation rates were 25.8%, 26.5% and 17.5%, respectively, and detection rates for advanced neoplasia were comparable at about 1%.

In the 2012 report of the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (ongoing telephone survey of US adults), 40.0% to 76.4% of adults aged 50 to 75 years received a CRC screening on the basis of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation for states and territories.

In a German study, 17.2% of eligible women and 15.5% of eligible men aged 55 to 74 years participated in colonoscopy screening. The adenoma detection rate was 19.4% and was higher in men than women (25.8% vs. 16.7%). Advanced adenomas were found in 6.4% of patients and carcinomas in 0.9%; most cancer was diagnosed at an early stage (I, 47.3%; II, 22.3%; III, 20.7%; IV, 9.6%).

In a large Spanish screening trial of 57,404 individuals, fecal occult blood testing every 2 years was more acceptable to patients than colonoscopy and yielded the same percentage of CRC (0.1%). Colonoscopy identified significantly more advanced adenomas (1.9% vs. 0.9%) and non-advanced adenomas (4.2% vs. 0.4%).

Racial disparity exists for use of colonoscopy. In a study of Medicare beneficiaries, colonoscopy use was higher in whites vs. blacks and Hispanics (40.7%, 35.0%, and 28.7% respectively). Availability of colonoscopists or PCPs did not attenuate these disparities.

In a review of a 2-year database of colonoscopy, 15% of the 1905 patients were over age 80 years. The pathology rate was higher in this group (72% vs. 59%) including cancer in 44 patients (15.2%). However, only half underwent surgery and survival was not statistically better among those undergoing surgery vs. not undergoing surgery (31 (IQR 12-38) months vs. 16 (IQR 5-31) months, respectively).

Barriers and facilitators: Reported barriers to colonoscopy include the laxative bowel preparation, anxiety, anticipation of pain, feelings of embarrassment and vulnerability, fear of finding cancer, and inadequate knowledge about the procedure and screening. Physician endorsement, having a family history of cancer, knowing someone with cancer, and perceived accuracy of the test were facilitators to colonoscopy.

Screening for CRC has been shown to reduce mortality from the disease with an estimated 10,000 deaths prevented each year if all adults aged ≥50 years were offered CRC screening (cost of $11,900 per life year saved).
Colon cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death with over 140,000 cases diagnosed each year and over 50,000 deaths.
In one study, the likelihood of dying from CRC was lower among persons who had ever undergone colonoscopy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.32; 95% CI, 0.24-0.45) or flexible sigmoidoscopy.

Authors, using a statistical (Markov) model, found colonoscopy to be more effective than other screening approaches, including no screening, in increasing life expectancy, decreasing colorectal cancer incidence and mortality, and decreasing costs. This model did not address the potential harms of testing.

Interestingly, a higher adenoma detection rate by a gastroenterologist is associated with a lower rate of CRC and death. Professional societies recommend a detection rate of at least 15% for female patients and 25% for male patients.
The addition of simethicone to PEG with ascorbic acid improved cleansing and lessened gastrointestinal symptoms in one RCT.
The colonoscope is a 120 cm flexible fiberoptic camera that allows both visualization of the colon as well as performance of diagnostic and therapeutic intervention.
The patient must undergo a bowel preparation the night before the procedure to removal all stool prior to the procedure to insure adequate visualization of the colon.

A telephone call on the day before colonoscopy with re-education on proper technique improved the quality of bowel preparation in one study and resulted in a higher polyp detection rate (38.0% vs. 24.7%).

For inpatients, a nurse-delivered educational intervention resulted in a higher proportion of colonoscopies with adequate bowel preparation (83.1% vs. 69.3% in the control group) in an RCT including 190 consecutive inpatients.
A smartphone education intervention reduced embarrassment and improved bowel preparation and satisfaction with care in an RCT of 150 patients receiving colonoscopy.

In an RCT of 306 patients scheduled for colonoscopy, those randomized to either domperidone group or sulpiride, two dopamine-2 receptor antagonist antiemetics, completed PEG better and had fewer abdominal discomforts and less severe nausea and abdominal fullness than those in the control group. In addition, the quality of bowel preparation was better in the intervention groups.
The combination of magnesium citrate and senna is recommended for children.

A meta-analysis of different bowel preparations found no differences between NaP and PEG, although the latter appeared more effective than non-NaP preparations and was more effective in proximal bowel clearance. Low-volume PEG containing ascorbic acid had comparable efficacy and tolerability to 2 L of split-dose PEG plus bisacodyl. For same-day cleansing before colonoscopy, sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and citric acid was comparable to PEG.

In one RCT, split dosing of picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and citric acid solution, a small-volume agent for colon cleansing, was better than traditional dosing for cleansing the right colon; both preparations were well tolerated. In a meta-analysis of 47 trials, split-dose regimens increased the quality of colon cleansing and were preferred by patients compared with day-before preparations. In a recent RCT, 2 L spit-dose preparation vs. single-dose bowel preparation resulted in decreased intensity and duration of BMs, less patient inconvenience, improved bowel preparation, and increased sessile-serrated polyp detection rates (9.9% vs. 2.4%), but no difference in adenoma detection rates.

Similar bowel cleanliness was also shown comparing PEG low-volume same-day dosing (15 mg bisacodyl the day before, 2 L the morning of the procedure), low-volume split-dose (15 mg bisacodyl the day before, 1 L + 1 L), or high-volume split-dose (2 L + 2 L) in a RCT of 1,750 subjects undergoing colonoscopy in Canadian endoscopy units. Willingness to repeat and tolerability were superior with the low-volume same-day regimen.
In a single-blind, multicenter, noninferiority study, cleansing success was high and equivalent using split-dose PEG-ascorbate vs. split-dose oral sulfate tablets (89% and 92%, respectively).

Authors of a systematic review of adverse events following bowel preparation found 171 cases of renal failure reported to the FDA following use of NaP and 10 following PEG. They concluded that although adverse events following bowel preparation are uncommon, they are potentially serious.

With respect to diet, authors of a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs found that similar effects of a clear-liquid or low-residue diet in bowel preparation quality, efficacy of colon cleansing, side effects, and compliance with the recommended dietary regime. Patients preferred the low-residue diet. These findings of similar effectiveness but better tolerability (RR 0.92; 95% CI, 0.85-0.99) and willingness to repeat a low-residue diet were also reported in a recent meta-analysis of 16 studies with 3413 subjects.

In another RCT, sodium picosulfate with a prepackaged low-residue, one-day diet had a higher success rate and fewer adverse effects than 4-L PEG for bowel preparation. Sodium picosulfate bowel preparations, however, lead to more hyponatremia than PEG, with an absolute risk increase of 0.05% (95% CI, 0.04%-0.06%).
On arrival to the endoscopy suite, the patient should undergo informed consent. Following consent, patients are sedated using standard conscious sedation protocols.

In a meta-analysis of 36 studies with 3918 patients, conscious sedation resulted in higher patient satisfaction and willingness to repeat the examination. Midazolam versus diazepam was associated with greater patient satisfaction and less memory of the endoscopy and propofol versus midazolam was associated with greater patient satisfaction and less memory of the endoscopy.

Authors of a 2025 Cochrane review concluded that propofol for sedation resulted in faster recovery and discharge times than traditional agents and increased patient satisfaction, confirming earlier studies.

In an RCT of 186 patients, investigators found etomidate sedation noninferior to propofol with respect to patient satisfaction. There were more cardiopulmonary adverse events in the propofol group (27.7% vs. 14.1% with etomidate), including hypoxia, hypo or hypertension, brady or tachycardia and arrythmia, but myoclonus occurred in 12.1% (11/92) in the etomidate group.
The addition of ketamine to propofol for sedation during colonoscopy resulted in less respiratory depression and hypotension, but caused more impairment in cognitive function.
In a small RCT, use of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) reduced pain by 50% or more compared with no intervention or sham TENS intervention in unsedated colonoscopy.

The patient is placed in the left lateral decubitus position with knees pulled forward. The provider performs a rectal examination for any palpable masses or lesions and then inserts the colonoscope. The scope is held in the left hand upright with the palm at the back of the controls to allow the fingers access to the buttons in the front and the dials on the side. The right hand is used to advance the scope and rotate the scope left and right. "Driving" the scope with these two hands approach allows the operator maximum control. Once in the rectum, insufflate the colon by covering the bottom blue air button. The scope is then advanced with a slow 360° inspection of the lumen.

Small movements on dials will make large movements of the tip of the scope. When approaching luminal curves, such as in the sigmoid colon, advance the scope almost to touching the forward wall of the colon before beginning to turn right or left. Most providers make the mistake of turning too soon and get caught in the folds of the curve. Use the suction button to remove excessive air from the colon and to relieve cramping and the water button, to wash and clear the scope tip.

The colonoscope should be advanced while noting the anatomy of each section of the colon. The rectum has large dilated veins in the mucosal wall, the sigmoid has multiple turns, the splenic flexure once trespassed opens to triangular folds of the transverse colon, the hepatic flexure is marked by a bluish hue on the mucosal wall, the ileocecal valve is yellowish and floppy and the proximal colon ends with the cecum, a terminal sac which usually has a slit-like appendiceal orifice.

Operators should be able to recognize and use anatomic landmarks for description of location of colonic abnormalities instead of centimeters of scope length which is often inaccurate due to looping of the scope in the sigmoid colon. The duration of the entire procedure should be documented including time to cecum and time for withdrawal of scope.

Once in the rectum, the scope is "retro-flexed" in order to be able to visualize the rectum. In the rectum, the large dial is moved either to the fully up or fully down position and the scope is advanced against the lateral wall of the rectum causing the tip of the scope to turn back on itself. If paradoxical motion does occur, the scope is advanced but moves backward instead, looping has occurred. Slowly withdraw the scope until one-to-one movement forward is re-established. Alternative techniques include jiggling the scope as it is advanced, having an assistant apply abdominal pressure and turning the patient from the left lateral decubitus position onto their abdomen with their arms above their head in a "superman" position. Pressure and position changes allow abdominal compression which may minimize looping.

Authors of a prospective study found that at least 6 minutes is needed to ensure adequate visualization of the colonic mucosa for abnormalities. Longer mean withdrawal times are associated with higher adenoma detection rates (3.6% per minute; 95% CI, 2.4%-4.8%). The adjusted cancer incidence rate ratio for withdrawal times of <6 minutes in this study was 2.3 (95% CI, 1.5-3.4). Therefore, providers should slowly withdraw the scope to insure visualization of the entire colonic mucosa.
Segmental withdrawal during screening colonoscopy was not better than standard withdrawal of at least 6 or 8 minutes on adenoma detection rate in one RCT.
Instructions to purposely seek colorectal polyps did not result in more polyps detected compared with routine colonoscopy in one RCT.

Other quality indicators include cecal intubation rates with proof by photo documentation of cecum, ileocecal valve and appendiceal orifice and adenoma detection rates. Photographic documentation should occur for any abnormality found as well as prebiopsy and postbiopsy. Many operators document visualization of the cecum and appendiceal orifice as well as retroflexion at the rectum.

In one screening population of 605 adults, computed tomographic colonography (CTC or "virtual colonoscopy") without prior laxative preparation was as good as colonoscopy for ruling out clinically relevant (10 mm or larger) adenomatous polyps. Comparability of these two procedures was demonstrated in one additional RCT. In one study, more than half of the patients with CRC symptoms, however, were found to have extracolonic pathologies by CTC; the proportion of patients with extracolonic malignancies 1 year after CTC exam, however, was not significantly greater than after barium enema or colonoscopy. In the most recent RCT of 1,276 colonoscopy and 982 CTC invitees, the detection rate of high-risk sessile serrated polyps was significantly higher with colonoscopy than CTC (3.1% vs. 0.4%).
CTC may be useful in the evaluation of patients with chronic constipation over colonoscopy due to a high failure rate in using colonoscopy.

In a retrospective study, CTC for screening resulted in a similar positive predictive value for CRC of 2.7% using a 6-mm-threshold compared to 1.9% following multitarget stool DNA testing, although rates of detection of advanced neoplasia were higher with CTC (5% vs. 2.7%, respectively). The positive predictive value for CRC was higher, at 5.2%, using a 10-mm-threshold.

In a study of patients with a positive FIT test, CTC performed similarly to colon capsule endoscopy (CEE) in detecting advanced CRC, but CEE was more sensitive for detecting significant neoplastic lesions; the sensitivity of CCE and CTC was 96.1% and 79.3%, respectively.

Authors of a review of CTC studies from Europe reported a screening participation rate for CTC of 25% to 34% (similar to FIT and higher than colonoscopy) and a CRC and advanced adenoma detection rate of 5.1% to 6.1% (higher than that of one round of fecal testing, similar to that of sigmoidoscopy and lower than that of colonoscopy).

In chromoscopy, also called chromoscopic colonoscopy or chromoendoscopy, endoscopists use an indigo carmine dye during extubation that may increase detection of neoplastic lesions. In an RCT with 1008 patients, there was a significantly increased detection of adenomas (46.2% vs. 36.3%) and a trend toward increased detection of advanced adenomas (103 vs. 81). Mean extubation times were 1.5 minutes longer. In a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs of patients with ulcerative colitis, chromoendoscopy had a pooled sensitivity of 83.3% (95% CI, 35.9%-99.6%) and specificity of 91.3% (95% CI, 43.8%-100%) for detection of dysplasia.

In a multinational RCT of 1205 patients undergoing CRC screening or surveillance colonoscopies, use of 200 mg per-oral methylene blue resulted in an absolute 8.5% increase in adenoma detection rate compared with placebo (56.29% vs. 47.81%; OR 1.46; 95% CI, 1.09-1.96). Adverse events occurred in 0.7% with no differences between groups.

Narrow-band imaging is endoscopy using narrowed blue, red, and green color bands of the spectrum to image distinct levels of mucosa and increase contrast between the epithelial surface and the subjacent vascular network. Authors of a Cochrane review of 11 RCTs found no significant difference between high definition white light colonoscopy and narrow band imaging colonoscopy in the number of patients identified with at least one colorectal polyp or colorectal adenoma. Two other meta-analyses reported similar findings, as did one RCT. However, continued development of different types of narrow band imaging may result in reliable optical diagnosis for colonic lesions without histopathological testing. These techniques still have a relatively low negative predictive value (65.9%-86.5%). Currently, polyp endoscopic classification is not accurate enough to forego histopathological assessment.

In a Spanish cohort study of 1634 consecutive patients, use of the Narrow-Band Imaging International Colorectal Endoscopic classification system along with morphologic features of pedunculated, ulcerated, depressed areas or nodular mixed type resulted in >96% specificity for identifying invasive polyps that are likely endoscopically unresectable. Sensitivity of the classification system alone was 58.4%.

Linked color imaging, a technique to enhance color contrast during virtual chromoendoscopy, was shown in one RCT of 1278 patients who underwent colonoscopy to significantly increase adenoma detection rate and polyp detection rate over the white-light colonoscopy group (34.4% vs. 26.8% and 53.3% vs. 46.4%, respectively).
Wide-field imaging following administration of a fluorescently-labeled peptide may be useful for identification of sessile serrated adenomas during routine colonoscopy.

High-resolution microendoscopy, an optical technology that allows for subcellular imaging, had high sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value (94%, 95% and 87%, respectively) compared to white-light endoscopy for identifying neoplastic colorectal polyps.
Full-spectrum endoscopy is a technologic advancement that provides a 330 degree field of view vs. 170 degrees for standard colonoscopy. This technology may lower the missed adenoma rate.

Confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) is a technique that allows simultaneous in vivo histologic assessment of the mucosa with a laser microscope during endoscopy following intravenous contrast administration. In one study with two experienced colonoscopists examining 64 patients, accuracy of CLE for both observers (66.7% and 71.9%) was significantly lower than accuracy of chromoendoscopy or narrow band imaging. The majority of CLE videos demonstrated insufficient quality in more than half of the recording time and no histology was shown at all on the video in 19 lesions (12%).
A variable stiffness colonoscope compared with the standard colonoscope in one study was associated with a higher cecal intubation rate, less abdominal pain, and decreased need for sedation.
A fitted abdominal corset during colonoscopy was shown in one study to reduce pain and decrease cecal intubation time, the need for extra manual compression, and change of position.

In a Cochrane review of 14 studies, use of a transparent cap on the end of the colonoscope resulted in a slightly faster cecal intubation time and possibly better polyp detection and less pain. In a larger meta-analysis of 12 studies on the same topic, authors concluded that cap-assisted colonoscopy vs. standard colonoscopy detected significantly more patients with polyps (OR 1.13) and had a significantly higher cecal intubation rate (OR 1.36). Time to cecal intubation was similar.
In a meta-analysis of 13 studies on colonoscopy, use of CO2 insufflation during the procedure caused less postprocedural pain and bowel distension than air insufflation.

In another meta-analysis, water infusion vs. air insufflation improved cecal intubation, reduced abdominal pain, and increased patients' willingness to repeat the procedure. In a Chinese RCT with 3,303 patients, water exchange (water infusion with water removal primarily during insertion) vs. air insufflation increased adenoma detection rates (18.3% vs. 13.4%, respectively for a RR of 1.45; 95% CI, 1.20-1.75). In a case series, water infusion was not associated with electrolyte disturbance within 10 min after procedure completion and most of the infused water was removed by suction.

Adding intravenous cimetropium bromide, an antispasmodic agent, after cecal intubation did not improve polyp and adenoma detection in the colorectum and right colon during colonoscope withdrawal in one RCT.

Computer-aided detection-assisted (CADe) colonoscopy was better than routine white-light colonoscopy for reducing the overall miss rate of adenomas (12.98%, 95% CI, 9.08%-16.88%) vs. 45.90%, 95% CI, 39.65%-52.15%). In this study, 369 patients were randomly assigned to received either CADe colonoscopy or routine colonoscopy first, followed immediately by the other procedure.
Having a nurse participate in the colonoscopy increased the polyp detection rate in a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs with a RR of 1.16; 95% CI, 1.05-1.27).
In two different meta-analyses, music played during the procedure was associated with reduced procedure time and amount of sedation in one and improved overall experience in the other.
Use of a relaxation intervention with a smartphone reduced reported pain and distention scores and improved satisfaction with colonoscopy in one RCT.

A Cochrane review found that colonoscopists who trained with simulation and virtual reality trainers had slightly better competency ratings compared with those who trained in the traditional apprenticeship and observation only modalities.

In an RCT, position changes during colonoscope withdrawal including use of the left lateral position for visualization of the cecum, ascending colon, and hepatic flexure; supine position for visualization of the transverse colon: and right lateral position for visualization of the splenic flexure, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum vs. the standard left lateral position for the entire procedure resulting in a higher rate of adenoma detection of 42.4% vs. 33.0%, respectively. The difference in detection rate was significant only for endoscopists with a relatively low baseline detection rate.
In another RCT, right-sided positioning at the start of colonoscopy resulted in less time to reach the cecum and greater patient comfort.

In a meta-analysis of 12 studies with over 18,000 patients of colonoscopies by primary care physicians, the mean estimated adenoma and adenocarcinoma detection rates were 28.9% (95% CI, 20.4-39.3) and 1.7% (95% CI, 0.9-3.0), respectively, and the mean estimated reach-the-cecum rate was 89.2% (95% CI, 80.1-94.4). The major complication rate was 0.04% (95% CI, 0.01-0.07) and there were no deaths.

A 2024 study found similar quality and polyp detection rates among family physicians, gastroenterologists, and general surgeons performing colonoscopies at two academic medical centers in Texas and North Dakota.
Polyps, the major target of the procedure, are often mucosal colored, occasionally bleeding growths encountered on the walls of the colon. They may be flat, raised or pedunculated.

In a pooled analysis of 8 tandem (i.e., 2 colonoscopy procedures) RCTs of screening or diagnostic colonoscopies, of polyps/adenomas were identified in almost half (49.8%). Half of the lesions were right-sided. Risk factors for missed adenomas were larger size, form (flat) and female patient but not location.
Prevalence of polyps on screening colonoscopy does not appear to differ by black or white race (6.57% and 6.2%, respectively), based on a meta-analysis of 9 studies with 302,128 individuals.

Biopsy techniques depend on polyp size, characteristics and location of the polyp. Removal of polyps may occur by cold, hot, or snare biopsy. Polyps must occasionally be injected, either to elevate the base for easier biopsy, to inject epinephrine to stop bleeding or to inject dye to locate the lesion for future testing.
Random biopsies in patients with ulcerative colitis appear to be of low yield for neoplasia.
Endoscopic full thickness resection of colonic lesions is under investigation. The ability to successfully close the defect is the major obstacle.
The modified handling of serrated polyps immediately after polypectomy by flattening and enclosing them in a paper envelope before being placed in formalin improved histopathologic interpretation.

Minor complications include abdominal discomfort or cramps during and after the procedure, rectal irritation from the bowel preparation, change in bowel habits, and infection. More serious complications include bleeding and bowel perforation. Rare complications are death and splenic trauma.

The risk of perforation is 1 in 500, and the risk of death is 1 in 5000. Perforation and bleeding risk appear higher for patients who have had large polypectomies or biopsies or are older and have medical disease states that could affect rates of healing and hemostasis. In one case-control study, large size (13% increased risk for every 1 mm increase in polyp diameter) and location in the right hemicolon (OR 4.67; 95% CI, 1.88-11.61) were risk factors for delayed hemorrhage after colonoscopic polypectomy.

Perforation requires close observation and rarely surgical intervention and is heralded by persistent abdominal pain post procedure. Bleeding may require direct visualization and injection of epinephrine into the bleeding site. Patients should be advised of these complications prior to the procedure and given written material postprocedure with detailed information about signs and symptoms for which to call.

In a Dutch study of 1140 patients, most undergoing diagnostic colonoscopy, followed up at 30 days post-procedure, 15 patients had definitely or possibly related major adverse events (1.3% including 4 episodes of rectal bleeding and one perforation) and almost one third had minor adverse events definitely or possibly related to colonoscopy (primarily abdominal discomfort or cramps [n = 195], rectal blood loss [n = 64] and change in bowel habits [n = 62]).

Authors of a systematic review of 21 studies of colonoscopy found pooled prevalences of post-colonoscopy bleeding of 2.6/1,000 (95% CI, 1.7-3.7), perforation of 0.5/1,000 (95% CI, 0.4-0.7), and mortality of 2.9/100,000 (95% CI, 1.1-5.5) colonoscopies. This translates into 50 perforations, 260 bleeds, and 3 deaths for every 100,000 procedures. Adding a biopsy increased rates of perforation to 0.8/1,000 (95% CI, 0.6-1.0) with a post-polypectomy bleeding rate of 9.8/1,000 (95% CI, 7.7-12.1).

In a Canadian study of 97,091 persons who had an outpatient colonoscopy, the pooled rates of colonoscopy-related bleeding and perforation were 1.64/1000 and 0.85/1000, respectively. The death rate was approximately 1/14,000. Older age, male sex, having a polypectomy, and having the colonoscopy performed by a low-volume endoscopist were associated with increased odds of bleeding or perforation.

Splenic trauma is also rare. In a review of the literature, 77 cases were identified with isolated splenic trauma. Patients presented with intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Nonoperative management in 25 patients was associated with a high failure rate in 11 patients, requiring a salvage procedure. Surgical management and proximal splenic artery embolization both appear effective, with similar hospital length of stay.

A 2025 study considered the risk of harms from overuse of screening colonoscopy (screening colonoscopy done outside of guidelines or recommendations). They estimated 1798 and 2258 bowel perforations and between 7257 and 9616 severe bleeds would occur in the US annually due to overuse of screening colonoscopy.

Follow-up depends on the findings during the procedure. In an average risk patient, where no polyps were detected and the bowel preparation was good, consensus recommendations allow a 10-year interval between colonoscopies. This interval was confirmed in a recent Polish study of 165,887 low-risk patients aged 50 years to 66 years with a single negative screening colonoscopy; rates of subsequent CRC and related mortality following high-quality colonoscopy was not different in the 10- to 17-year interval compared with the 0- to 5-year and 5- to 10-year intervals. If bowel preparation was poor and visualization was difficult, repeat can occur as early as 1-year interval.

It is estimated that 22% to 28% of polyps and 20% to 24% of adenomas are missed during a single colonoscopy. In a meta-analysis of 43 papers with over 15,000 tandem colonoscopies, investigators found missed rates of 26% for adenomas (95% CI, 23%-30%), 9% for advanced adenomas (95% CI, 4%-16%), and 27% for serrated polyps (95% CI, 16%-40%).

Patients with polyps found to be precancerous, tubular, tubulovillous or villous should be reexamined in 3 years provided that bowel preparation was adequate. Controversy exists on follow-up of normal hyperplastic polyps, as many still repeat colonoscopy in 3 years. The AGA 2022 guidelines do not provide recommendations on follow-up for high-risk adenomas.

In a British study of post-polypectomy patients aged 60 to 72 years who underwent annual FIT testing and repeat colonoscopy at 3 years, authors concluded that annual FIT could reduce colonoscopies by 71%, significantly cutting costs, but could miss 30% to 40% of CRCs and 40% to 70% of advanced adenomas.

Authors of a systematic review found that, at 5-year follow-up, patients with low-risk adenomas identified at initial colonoscopy were more likely to develop advanced adenomas than those with no polyps identified (4.9% vs. 3.3%, respectively), but their overall risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) and CRC-related mortality may be lower than in the general population.

The finding of high-risk adenomas on colonoscopy is a predictor of subsequent high-risk adenomas. In a cohort study of 891 patients who had 3 or more colonoscopies, high-risk adenomas were found in 12.8%. Compared with those who had no adenomas on both previous exams, participants with high-risk adenomas on the first exam were at increased risk for a high-risk adenoma at the third examination, conducted after a negative second examination at 3 years (OR 3.41; 95% CI, 1.28-9.08), 5 years (OR 3.14; 95% CI, 1.49-6.61), and 7 years (OR 2.89; 95% CI, 1.08-7.74).

Norwegian national guidelines recommended a repeat colonoscopy in 10 years for patients with a high-risk adenoma (multiple adenomas, villous growth pattern, or high-grade dysplasia) or 5 years if they had 3 or more adenomas, but no regular surveillance for those with a low-risk adenoma. Based on a Norwegian study using comprehensive national cancer and death registries, the risk of dying due to CRC was significantly lower in patients who had a low-risk polyp removed (standardized mortality ratio [SMR] = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.63-0.88), but was significantly higher in patients with a high-risk polyp (SMR = 1.19; 1.02-1.31). This finding supports their decision to omit surveillance in low-risk patients and suggests a need for enhanced surveillance in high-risk patients.

In a follow-up study of 15,935 patients with a polyp of mass identified on screening sigmoidoscopy, initial colonoscopy identified 2882 patients (18.1%) with advanced adenoma and 5068 (31.8%) with nonadvanced adenoma; the remaining 50.1% had no adenoma identified. The cumulative incidence of CRC over 15 years was twice as high in the advanced adenoma group (2.9%; 95% CI, 2.3%-3.7%) and similar in the other two groups at 1.4% (1.1%-1.8%) and 1.2% (1.0%-1.6%).
The European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy recommends that patients with 10 or more adenomas be referred for genetic counseling.
Findings of cancerous polyps require immediate follow-up usually with resection and then repeat colonoscopy in 1 year. Further follow-up is determined based on findings from that visit.

For survivors of CRC, the American Society of Clinical Oncology endorses the Cancer Care Ontario Guideline which recommends a surveillance colonoscopy 1 year after the initial surgery and then every 5 years, based on the findings of the previous one. They also recommend obtaining a medical history, physical examination, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) testing every 3 to 6 months for 5 years, depending on risk of recurrence and patient’s functional status, and a chest and abdominal CT scan yearly for 3 years.

However, in a study of 1202 patients following curative surgery for CRC, intensive follow-up with regular CT and CEA testing, or both, and colonoscopy at 2 years resulted in more patients undergoing repeat surgery but no reduction in overall mortality or disease-specific mortality over minimal follow-up with colonoscopy offered at 5 years.

Authors of a systematic review and metanalysis of 27 studies, with data on 15,803 index patients with CRCs, reported recurrent CRCs in 454 patients. Two hundred and ninety-six CRCs occurred at non-anastomotic locations over more than 16 years (cumulative incidence 2.2%; 95% CI, 1.8%-2.9%). The risk of CRC at a non-anastomotic location was significantly reduced after 36 months post resection. One hundred and fifty-eight CRCs were located at anastomoses (cumulative incidence of 2.7%; 95% CI, 1.9%-3.9%) and these recurrences decreased significantly after 24 months.

Among 3296 patients from 17 studies with CT-confirmed acute left-sided diverticulitis, follow-up colonoscopy within 1 year found a pooled rate of CRC of 0.5% for uncomplicated cases and 8.4% among those with complicated cases (accompanied by abscess, perforation, or fistula).

Older age was associated with a higher polyp recurrence rate at 3-years following removal of one or more sporadic colorectal adenomas during colonoscopy (recurrence rate 35% if over age 70 years vs. 19% if aged 50 years or less).

Age of the patient can also be used to estimate the risk of metachronous cancer development—multiple primary tumors that develop at intervals—to determine the optimal colonoscopy follow-up interval. For patients who are <65 years at the time of the primary curative resection, there is a 2% 5-year risk of metachronous cancer while for those >75 years, there is less than a 2% 10-year risk.

Typical fees for this procedure range by location, office or hospital-based and regionally. Typical fees vary with office-based providers charging a professional fee of $350 to $500 including conscious sedation. Hospital-based procedures have two fees, $350 to $750 for professional fees and $350 to $1000 for facility fees. Biopsies and use of sclerotherapy increase the fee charged.
Average cost reported in 2013 on Costhelper.com was $3081.00 for patients not covered by insurance.

Patients will require time off work. Patients will take the bowel preparation the day before the procedure. Most patients can do this in the evening hours and thus do not require work excuse. The day of the procedure due to the use of conscious sedation, patients must be accompanied by someone who can drive them home and should be excused from work for that day. They may return to work the next day.

Conscious sedation protocols should be followed requiring a person dedicated to monitoring the patient during the procedure, giving IV medications and starting IVs. Nurses should understand the procedure and be expected to help with biopsies and with patient position changes as needed.
